lessons.title: What Combinatorial Optimization Problems Look Like

slots.practicalActivity: Compute 2^n by hand for n=25 decision variables (the way the lesson computes it for n=20, 50, and 300), then pick a real combinatorial problem from your own life or work that is NOT one of the lesson's three examples (portfolio selection, routing, scheduling) and write its decision variables, objective function, and constraints in the same three-ingredient format the lesson uses.
slots.deliverable: Your 2^25 calculation plus a written three-part problem statement (decision variables / objective / constraints) for a self-chosen real combinatorial problem.

slots.practicalActivity: Invent your own upper-triangular 2x2 Q matrix (different numbers than the lesson's Q=[[-5,2],[0,-3]]), hand-evaluate f(x1,x2) at all four binary assignments, and identify the minimum. Then add the penalty term P(x1+x2-1)^2 with P=10 for an 'exactly one selected' constraint and recompute all four totals to see whether the winning assignment changes.
slots.deliverable: Your own Q matrix, a 4-row table of unconstrained f(x) values, and a second 4-row table of penalty-adjusted totals, with the winning assignment stated in both cases.

slots.practicalActivity: Using the substitution s_i = 1 - 2x_i, convert the QUBO f(x1,x2) = 6x1 - 4x2 + 3x1x2 (your own coefficients, different from the lesson's worked example) into its Ising Hamiltonian H(s) by hand, showing every algebraic step. Then verify your conversion by evaluating both f(x) and H(s) at all four binary assignments and confirming they match exactly.
slots.deliverable: Your worked algebra deriving H(s) from f(x), plus a 4-row table confirming f(x) and H(s) agree at every assignment.

slots.practicalActivity: Add a diagonal edge (0,2) to the 4-cycle graph from this lesson, making a 5-edge graph that is no longer perfectly bipartite in the simple alternating way. Recompute, edge by edge, the cut value for x=(1,0,1,0) across all 5 edges, then test at least two other assignments to find the best cut you can for this new graph.
slots.deliverable: A per-edge cut table for all 5 edges under x=(1,0,1,0), plus your best-found assignment and its total cut value for the modified graph.

slots.practicalActivity: Design your own 5-node graph (at least 5 edges, different from this lab's triangle-plus-bridges graph), build its upper-triangular Q matrix by hand directly from the edge list using the lesson's degree-based diagonal rule, evaluate one candidate assignment using the matrix form f(x) = Σ Q_ii x_i + Σ Q_ij x_i x_j, and brute-force check enough assignments to state the true maximum cut with confidence.
slots.deliverable: Your Q matrix, one fully hand-evaluated f(x) on a candidate assignment, and the brute-force-confirmed true optimum with the winning assignment(s) stated.

slots.practicalActivity: Sketch the 3-part QAOA circuit skeleton (Hadamards, one cost/mixer layer, measurement) for the single-edge 2-qubit Max-Cut problem from this lesson, labeling exactly where γ and β enter the circuit. Then, using the lesson's two reported results (expected cost 1.0 at γ=π/2, β=π/8 versus ≈0.519 at γ=0.1, β=0.1), compute what fraction of the perfect result (1.0) each setting actually achieves.
slots.deliverable: Your labeled circuit sketch plus the two fraction-of-perfect calculations (1.0/1.0 and 0.519/1.0) stated explicitly.

slots.practicalActivity: By hand, evaluate the cost Hamiltonian H_C = ½(I - Z_0Z_1) on all four 2-qubit basis states |00⟩, |01⟩, |10⟩, |11⟩, using the fact that Z has eigenvalue +1 on |0⟩ and -1 on |1⟩, and confirm you recover the lesson's stated values 0, 1, 1, 0. Then write out the 2x2 matrices for Z and X and compute the commutator [Z,X] = ZX - XZ directly to confirm it is nonzero.
slots.deliverable: Your four hand-evaluated H_C values across the basis states, plus the explicit 2x2 commutator matrix computation showing [Z,X] ≠ 0.

slots.practicalActivity: The lesson states a p=5 (10-parameter) QAOA circuit needs about 20 extra circuit evaluations per gradient step under the parameter-shift rule. Redo this calculation by hand for p=8 and p=12, then estimate the total circuit evaluations a 50-iteration gradient-based optimization run would need at p=12.
slots.deliverable: Your evaluation-count calculations for p=8 and p=12, plus the estimated 50-iteration total at p=12.

slots.practicalActivity: Using the lesson's stated gate-fidelity range (99.0%-99.9%), estimate by hand the total surviving-probability of a depth-6 QAOA circuit if each layer adds roughly 8 two-qubit gates at 99.5% fidelity each (compute 0.995^48). Compare that accumulated error against the theoretical benefit of going from p=2 (ratio ≈0.9999) toward p=6.
slots.deliverable: Your 0.995^48 error calculation and a one-paragraph judgment on whether pushing to p=6 is worth it on today's noisy hardware given that number.

slots.practicalActivity: Take a new 4-node star graph (one center node connected to the other three: edges {(0,1),(0,2),(0,3)}) and find its true maximum cut by direct reasoning, since every edge shares node 0. Then compare the uniform pre-QAOA baseline (1/16 per basis state, since this is a 4-qubit problem) to the lesson's own 3-node path-graph probability table, writing out qualitatively how you'd expect a tuned QAOA circuit to reshape the star graph's distribution in a similar way.
slots.deliverable: Your stated true optimum for the star graph with reasoning, plus a short written comparison to the lesson's path-graph distribution shape.

slots.practicalActivity: Using the same method as this lesson, hand-diagonalize a new Hamiltonian H = Z + 2X (a different coefficient than the lesson's 0.5X) to find its exact eigenvalues via ±√(a²+b²). Then evaluate the trial ansatz's energy, cos(θ) + 2sin(θ), at θ = 0, π/4, π/2, π, and 3π/2, to see how close a simple angle scan gets to your exact ground energy.
slots.deliverable: Your exact eigenvalue calculation for H = Z + 2X, and a 5-row table of trial energies at the five tested angles.

slots.practicalActivity: Compute ⟨Z⟩ = cos(θ) by hand at three angles not shown in the lesson's table (θ = 3π/4, 5π/4, 7π/4), confirming the full range from +1 to -1 is swept by a single R_y rotation. Then write a structural explanation (2-3 sentences) of why a 2-qubit ansatz built only from independent single-qubit R_y rotations, with no CNOT gate, can never reach an entangled ground state no matter how its parameters are tuned.
slots.deliverable: Your 3-row ⟨Z⟩ table at the new angles, plus the written structural explanation naming the missing ingredient (an entangling gate).

slots.practicalActivity: Using H2's benchmark ground-state energy of approximately -1.137 Hartree and the chemical-accuracy threshold of 1.6 milli-Hartree, calculate by hand what percentage of the total energy that accuracy threshold represents. Then write two sentences distinguishing 'VQE reproduced H2's known energy' from 'VQE outperformed classical methods on an industrially relevant molecule,' citing the lesson's own LiH/BeH2 examples as evidence.
slots.deliverable: Your percentage calculation (1.6 mHartree relative to 1137 mHartree) plus the two-sentence distinction, each sentence citing a specific molecule named in the lesson.

slots.practicalActivity: Apply the lab's product-state test (v00·v11 =? v01·v10) to the vector (0.6, 0.3, 0.3, 0.6) to check whether it could represent a product (non-entangled) state. Then apply the same test to the normalized Bell state (1/√2, 0, 0, 1/√2) and explain why the result confirms it is maximally entangled.
slots.deliverable: Your two product-state test calculations (the 0.6/0.3/0.3/0.6 vector and the Bell state), each explicitly judged entangled or not with the arithmetic shown.

lessons.title: Portfolio Optimization as a QUBO Problem

slots.practicalActivity: Using r=[0.10, 0.07, 0.05] and the covariance matrix from this lesson, recompute the risk term (now 3·xᵗΣx instead of 0.5·xᵗΣx) for x=(1,1,0) and x=(1,0,1) at a much higher risk aversion q=3, recompute each total F(x), and determine whether (1,1,0) is still the winning choice.
slots.deliverable: Your two recomputed risk terms, the two recomputed F(x) totals at q=3, and a one-sentence verdict on whether the optimal pick changed from the lesson's q=0.5 result.

lessons.title: Quantum Amplitude Estimation for Risk Analysis

slots.practicalActivity: Using the scaling laws from this lesson (classical ~1/ε², quantum ~1/ε), compute the classical sample count and quantum oracle-query count needed for a new precision target, ε=0.0001, not shown in the lesson's table, and state the resulting speedup factor.
slots.deliverable: Your computed classical sample count, quantum query count, and speedup factor for ε=0.0001, laid out the same way as the lesson's table.

slots.practicalActivity: Using the same return distribution (μ=0.07, σ=0.15) from this lesson, compute the z-score and exact probability for a different loss threshold, P(return < -0.05), using the same (-threshold-μ)/σ method against the standard normal distribution. Compare your result to the lesson's own exact value for P(return < -0.10) of ≈0.12854.
slots.deliverable: Your z-score calculation, the resulting exact probability for the -5% threshold, and a one-sentence comparison to the lesson's -10% result.

lessons.title: Honest Limits of Quantum Finance Today

slots.practicalActivity: Find or recall one real quantum-computing press release or vendor claim about finance, optimization, or a speedup, and apply this lesson's four-question framework to it in writing: is the speedup theoretical or empirical, what problem size was actually tested, was the classical baseline a strong one, and was it run on a simulator or real hardware.
slots.deliverable: A short written evaluation of one real or recalled claim, answering all four framework questions explicitly, ending in a stated verdict on whether the claim holds up.

slots.practicalActivity: Using the 4-asset lab's r and Σ, rescale the risk terms for x=(1,1,0,0) and x=(1,0,0,1) down to risk aversion q=0.1 (risk term scales linearly with q, so rescale the given xᵗΣx values directly), recompute both F(x) totals, and determine whether the naive highest-return pick (1,1,0,0) now wins instead of the lab's q=1.0 answer of (1,0,0,1).
slots.deliverable: Your two rescaled risk terms, the two recomputed F(x) totals at q=0.1, and a one-sentence verdict on which assignment wins at this lower risk aversion.

lessons.title: Classical Optimization Baselines: Simulated Annealing & Solver-Style Methods
lessons.chapterTitle: Benchmarking Quantum Optimization vs. Classical Solvers

slots.practicalActivity: Using the simulated-annealing acceptance rule e^(Δ/T), compute by hand the probability of accepting a worsening move with Δ=-1 (cut drops by 1) at three temperatures: T=2.0 (early in the run), T=0.5 (mid-run), and T=0.05 (near the end of cooling), to see concretely how much less likely a worsening move becomes as the schedule cools.
slots.deliverable: Your three acceptance-probability calculations (T=2.0, T=0.5, T=0.05) with a one-sentence explanation of why the trend matters for SA eventually settling on a strong answer.

lessons.title: Designing a Fair Benchmark
lessons.chapterTitle: Benchmarking Quantum Optimization vs. Classical Solvers

slots.practicalActivity: Take the lesson's example claim — 'our QAOA implementation found a better Max-Cut solution than classical search in fewer iterations' — and write out specific follow-up questions you'd need answered under each of the lesson's four failure modes (weak baseline, query count without query cost, cherry-picked instance, excluded classical overhead) before accepting it as a fair benchmark.
slots.deliverable: A written list of specific follow-up questions, organized under each of the four named failure-mode headings.

lessons.title: Where Quantum Optimization Currently Stands
lessons.chapterTitle: Benchmarking Quantum Optimization vs. Classical Solvers

slots.practicalActivity: Write a short explanation (3-4 sentences) distinguishing the claim 'quantum advantage has been demonstrated for random circuit sampling' from 'quantum advantage has been demonstrated for combinatorial optimization.' Then invent one specific, realistic vendor claim about a quantum optimization advantage and explain, citing this lesson's criteria, what evidence it would need to meet before you'd accept it.
slots.deliverable: Your written distinction between the two advantage claims, plus your invented vendor-claim evaluation against this lesson's standard.

lessons.title: Benchmarking Lab
lessons.chapterTitle: Benchmarking Quantum Optimization vs. Classical Solvers

slots.practicalActivity: Using this lab's own comparison table (brute force, greedy, simulated annealing, and QAOA results on Instances A and B), write a critique explaining why presenting it as 'QAOA beats greedy and matches SA' would be incomplete or misleading, citing at least two of the earlier benchmark-fairness checks by name and pointing to the exact numbers in the table each one calls into question.
slots.deliverable: Your written critique citing two specific fairness checks by name and the exact table numbers each one implicates.

lessons.title: Capstone Kickoff: Choose a Real Optimization Problem

slots.practicalActivity: Add a fifth task of duration 6 hours to the model problem (d=[3,5,2,4,6], total=20) and determine, by checking combinations directly, whether the five tasks can be split into two perfectly equal 10-hour groups. Then run the lesson's three-part scoping checklist (stated objective, verifiable optimum, chosen classical baseline) against your own real capstone problem idea, in writing.
slots.deliverable: Your 5-task split result (a found 10-10 split, or a proof none exists) plus your own capstone problem's three-part scoping checklist answers.

lessons.title: Capstone: Build the Hybrid Optimization Workflow

slots.practicalActivity: Using d=[3,5,2,4], hand-verify the lesson's Ising Hamiltonian derivation (H(s) = 54 + 2Σd_i d_j s_i s_j) by directly evaluating both F(x) and H(s) at three bitstrings of your own choosing, confirming they agree exactly. Then, looking at the lesson's reported probability table, write in your own words why the circuit's expected-cost-minimizing angles didn't put the highest probability on the true optimal bitstrings.
slots.deliverable: Your three hand-verified (F(x), H(s)) pairs showing exact agreement, plus a written explanation of the expected-cost-vs-probability mismatch.

lessons.title: Capstone: Compare Against a Classical Baseline

slots.practicalActivity: Run the LPT heuristic by hand, step by step, on the new dataset d=[5,6,4,1,9,8] (total=33), recording each sort-and-assign decision. Then compare your LPT result's imbalance to the alternative split {9,8} versus {6,5,4,1} (imbalance=1), and determine which one actually wins.
slots.deliverable: Your full step-by-step LPT trace on the 6-task dataset, its resulting imbalance, and a stated verdict on whether LPT or the alternative split is better.

slots.practicalActivity: Using the ≈0.95% combined probability of observing a true-optimal bitstring from the earlier QAOA result, compute the expected number of measurement shots needed to see it at least once (1/p). Then write your own capstone's full five-section writeup (problem statement, formulation, methods compared, honest comparison, limitations and costs), using either your own problem from the kickoff lesson or the Number Partitioning example as the subject.
slots.deliverable: Your expected-shots calculation (~105) plus a complete five-section written capstone report covering problem statement, formulation, methods compared, honest comparison, and limitations/costs.

monthlyMilestoneContribution: After this course, a student can take a real combinatorial optimization or finance problem, formulate it as a QUBO, convert it to an Ising Hamiltonian, build and tune a QAOA or VQE circuit, and run a fair, honest benchmark against classical baselines like simulated annealing and LPT — including knowing precisely when and why quantum methods currently fall short of classical ones.
